overview.intro:
Chapter 17 covers cane and beet sugar, the other sugars and syrups (maple, glucose, fructose, lactose), molasses and sugar confectionery that contains no cocoa — hard candy, gummies, chewing gum and white chocolate. Its **92 tariff lines** split into two worlds. **Candy and most syrups** carry ordinary rates (Free to 12.2%). **Sugar** sits under the U.S. sugar program: a **tariff-rate quota** lets a fixed quantity in at a low rate — for raw sugar a per-kilogram rate that falls with the sugar's **polarity** — and everything above it pays 33.87¢ to 35.74¢ a kilogram.

The U.S. imported **$6.48B** of these goods in 2025; **Mexico** ($1.92B) and **Canada** ($1.18B) supplied 48%, mostly candy. On top of the base rate comes an **extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies (10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most others, more for China), with in-quota raw and refined sugar exempt; **Brazil** adds 25% on every line, in-quota sugar included. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico pay no Section 301 duty, but seven Canadian lactose, syrup and blend lines pay a 50% Section 338 duty and Canadian molasses is banned.

productGroups.label: Cane & beet sugar — raw, refined and flavored
productGroups.blurb: Raw and refined cane or beet sugar is a tariff-rate quota product, and its in-quota rate depends on the polarity (the sugar degree on the polarimeter). Raw cane sugar inside the WTO quota pays 1.4606¢/kg at 100°, 0.020668¢/kg less for each degree under 100 — about 1.38¢/kg at the usual 96°. Above the quota it pays 33.87¢/kg (raw cane) or 35.74¢/kg (beet and refined sugar). Flavored or colored sugar with over 65% or 10% sugar is 6% inside its quota and 33.9¢/kg + 5.1% above it.

productGroups.label: Other sugars & syrups — lactose, maple, glucose, fructose, invert sugar
productGroups.blurb: Maple syrup and maple sugar are Free (1702.20.40). Glucose syrup is 2.2¢/kg, fructose syrup 5.1%, chemically pure fructose 9.6%, lactose 6.4% and invert molasses 0.35¢ a liter. Blended syrups and sugar-rich articles made for further processing have quotas set at zero, so they pay the over-quota rate: 16.9¢ or 33.9¢ per kg of total sugars + 5.1%.

productGroups.label: Molasses
productGroups.blurb: Cane and beet molasses pay 0.35¢ a liter when imported to extract sugar or for human consumption, and 0.01¢ per kg of total sugars otherwise (mostly animal feed). Molasses from Canada can no longer be imported since September 29, 2026.

productGroups.label: Sugar confectionery — candy, chewing gum, white chocolate
productGroups.blurb: Candy without cocoa — hard candy, gummies, lollipops, marshmallows, licorice, white chocolate — is mostly 1704.90.35 at 5.6%. Chewing gum is 4%, candied nuts 4.5% and cough drops Free. Confections made for further processing with over 65% or 10% sugar are 12.2% inside their quota and 40¢/kg + 10.4% above it.

workedExamples.title: Raw cane sugar from the Philippines, inside the quota
workedExamples.body: The Philippines holds the second-largest raw cane sugar allocation for fiscal 2027 (154,386 metric tons raw value). Inside the quota the rate is 1.4606¢/kg less 0.020668¢/kg for each degree of polarity under 100. At 96°: 1.4606 − 4 × 0.020668 = 1.3779¢/kg, so 20,000 kg pays **$275.59**. 1701.14.10 is on the Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)), so nothing is added. The same sugar without a quota certificate enters under 1701.14.50 at 33.87¢/kg plus 12.5% of value — $6,774 plus $1,250 on a $10,000 shipment.

workedExamples.title: Hard candy from China
workedExamples.body: Hard candy, gummies and lollipops have a 5.6% general rate. China pays two Section 301 duties on top: +12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31) and +25% because 1704.90.35 is on List 3 (9903.88.03). That is **43.1%**: $21,550 on a $50,000 shipment. The same candy from Mexico is Free when it qualifies for USMCA (1704 needs only a change from another heading) and 15.6% when it does not.

workedExamples.title: Maple syrup from Canada
workedExamples.body: Pure maple syrup and maple sugar are Free under the general rate. Maple syrup is not on the Canada Section 338 lists, so a USMCA-qualifying shipment pays **nothing**. Syrup that does not qualify for USMCA pays the 10% Section 301 duty for Canada (9903.05.29). Blended maple syrups made for further processing are different: they fall on 1702.20.28 at 16.9¢ per kg of total sugars + 5.1%.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) sugar confectionery containing cocoa (heading 1806); (b) chemically pure sugars (other than sucrose, lactose, maltose, glucose and fructose) or other products of heading 2940; or (c) medicaments or other products of chapter 30.

**Subheading note 1.** For subheadings 1701.12, 1701.13 and 1701.14, "raw sugar" means sugar whose sucrose content by weight, in the dry state, corresponds to a polarimeter reading of less than 99.5 degrees.

**Subheading note 2.** Subheading 1701.13 covers only cane sugar obtained without centrifugation, with a polarimeter reading of 69° or more but less than 93°, containing only natural anhedral microcrystals surrounded by residues of molasses and other constituents of sugar cane.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**Note 1.** "Degree" in the rates of duty means sugar degree as determined by a polarimetric test — the polarity that the raw-sugar rates are graded by.

**Notes 2–4** define the articles with over 65% sugar (note 2), over 10% sugar (note 3) and blended syrups (note 4) that are not prepared for the final consumer.

**Note 5.** The WTO tariff-rate quotas: raw cane sugar (1701.13.10, 1701.14.10) of not less than 1,117,195 metric tons raw value a fiscal year, and other sugars, syrups and molasses (1701.12.10, 1701.91.10, 1701.99.10, 1702.90.10, 2106.90.44) of not less than 22,000 metric tons, set by the Secretary of Agriculture and allocated among countries by USTR. "Raw value" is the equivalent in sugar testing 96° by the polariscope.

**Note 6.** Raw cane sugar under 1701.13.20 and 1701.14.20 may be entered only to make polyhydric alcohols (not for use as a sugar substitute in food), to be refined and re-exported, or to substitute for domestic raw sugar that is exported — under USDA licenses.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 17 base rate changed: 90 of the 92 lines are the same, and the other 2 are new statistical splits of 1702.90.90 (certified organic and other) that carry their parent's 5.1%. The sugar quota system — in-quota and over-quota lines, the polarity-graded raw-sugar rates — is unchanged.

What changed came on top of the base rate, as extra duties set by country. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35%, Mexico +25%, Brazil +40%, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them — no sugar or candy line was on its exemption list — expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**; the in-quota raw and refined sugar lines are on its exemption list, the over-quota lines and candy are not. Brazil adds a separate **25%** on every Chapter 17 line, and since August 22, 2026 seven Canadian lactose and syrup lines pay a **50% Section 338 duty**, with Canadian molasses and invert molasses **banned** from September 29. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt from the Section 301 duty.** Sugar from Mexico remains under the **antidumping and countervailing duty suspension agreements**, continued for five more years in September 2025.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 17 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the older China Section 301 lists, the Canada Section 338 dairy-list duty and import ban, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, the sugar tariff-rate quotas and their FY 2027 allocations, and the suspension agreements on sugar from Mexico. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

The over-quota sugar lines, the general note 15 and re-export lines, syrups, molasses and candy are not on the list. Mexican sugar is Free under USMCA with no quantity limit (9823.09.01), but it is covered by the 2014 antidumping and countervailing duty suspension agreements (A-201-845, C-201-846), continued in September 2025: Mexican producers sell within export limits and above reference prices, and every entry needs a Mexican export license. changes.title: No Chapter 17 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 92 Chapter 17 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition, including the polarity-graded raw-sugar rates and every in-quota / over-quota pair. The two new statistical lines — 1702.90.90.20 (certified organic) and 1702.90.90.50 (other) — split 1702.90.90 and keep its 5.1% rate.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028. CAFTA-DR originating goods — including sugar entered under Nicaragua's FTA quota — are not covered (U.S. note 29). Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58), and its WTO raw sugar allocation is exempt from it.

changes.title: FY 2027 sugar quotas open
changes.detail: The fiscal 2027 tariff-rate quotas opened: raw cane sugar 1,117,195 metric tons raw value (the WTO minimum), refined sugar 22,000 MTRV (10,300 for Canada, 2,954 for Mexico, 7,090 first-come first-served, plus 1,656 of specialty sugar first-come first-served) and 64,709 metric tons of sugar-containing products under note 8 (59,250 for Canada). The same day USDA set the FY 2027 domestic overall allotment quantity at 10,574,850 short tons raw value, 85% of forecast U.S. consumption.

changes.title: Canadian molasses and invert molasses banned
changes.detail: Proclamation 11062 moved certain Canadian dairy-list products from the 50% Section 338 duty to an import ban for goods imported from 12:01 a.m. ET on September 29, 2026. In Chapter 17 that is invert molasses (1702.90.35) and the four molasses lines (1703.10.30, 1703.10.50, 1703.90.30, 1703.90.50); goods imported before that date and entered later still pay the 50%. The other seven Chapter 17 subheadings on the dairy list keep the 50% duty.

changes.title: Rest of the FY 2027 raw sugar quota allocated
changes.detail: USTR allocated the remaining 55,993 MTRV of the raw cane sugar quota among 28 countries, on top of the July allocations — for example +11,931 t for the Dominican Republic, +9,151 t for the Philippines and +5,626 t for Australia. Brazil and Mexico received no addition.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 dairy-list duty reaches twelve Chapter 17 subheadings
changes.detail: 50% on Canadian products on the dairy list (U.S. note 51(b)(2), 9903.03.13) took effect after the 3-day suspension lapsed. In Chapter 17 the list covers lactose (1702.11.00, 1702.19.00), blended syrups (1702.30.28, 1702.40.28, 1702.60.28, 1702.90.58), articles over 65% sugar (1702.90.68), invert molasses (1702.90.35) and molasses (1703.10.30, 1703.10.50, 1703.90.30, 1703.90.50). It applies even to goods that qualify for USMCA. Canadian sugar, maple syrup and candy are not on it.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover Chapter 17
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). The six in-quota raw and refined sugar subheadings — 1701.12.10, 1701.13.10, 1701.14.10, 1701.91.10, 1701.99.10 and 1702.90.10 — are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86); over-quota sugar, syrups, molasses and candy are not. EU goods pay 10% in total; Japan, South Korea and Switzerland 12.5% in total. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94), and a special rate under another FTA does not remove the duty (note 52(a)).

changes.title: FY 2027 sugar quota allocations by country
changes.detail: USTR allocated 1,061,202 MTRV of the 1,117,195 MTRV raw cane sugar quota among 39 countries — the Dominican Republic 189,343 t, the Philippines 145,235 t, Brazil 100,000 t, Australia 89,293 t, Guatemala 51,639 t, Argentina 46,260 t, Peru 44,108 t — and split the refined and sugar-containing product quotas. Imports from countries with an allocation need a certificate of quota eligibility.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). The exemption list in U.S. note 50(a)(ii) has no Chapter 17 subheading, so Brazilian sugar pays it even inside Brazil's raw cane sugar quota. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top, except on the note 52(b) in-quota sugar lines.

changes.title: Domestic sugar program extended through crop year 2031
changes.detail: USDA amended the sugar program rules (7 CFR part 1435) to carry out the One Big Beautiful Bill Act: the program — loans, marketing allotments and the import quotas that support it — runs through crop year 2031, with higher raw cane and refined beet sugar loan rates. Import tariffs did not change.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S, S+), Mexico's unlimited sugar access (9823.09.01) and Canada's USMCA sugar quotas (9823.09, 9823.10) still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 17 line was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: New annual reviews of the Mexico sugar agreements
changes.detail: Commerce opened the next administrative reviews of the sugar from Mexico suspension agreements: December 1, 2024 – November 30, 2025 (antidumping, A-201-845) and calendar 2025 (countervailing, C-201-846). Results are pending.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) makes the in-quota and general note 15 sugar lines and most candy Free for listed sub-Saharan countries; the over-quota sugar lines do not list D. GSP (SPI A, A*, A+) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Mexico sugar antidumping agreement review (2022–2023)
changes.detail: Commerce found the antidumping suspension agreement met the statutory requirements for December 2022 – November 2023, but that one producer group did not eliminate at least 85% of the dumping found in the investigation, and said it would take steps to remedy the noncompliance. The agreement stays in force.

changes.title: Mexico sugar suspension agreements continued
changes.detail: After the second five-year (sunset) reviews, the USITC found that ending the suspended investigations would likely lead to renewed injury, and Commerce continued both agreements. They cover raw and refined sugar of all polarities (1701 and 1702.90.40), set export limits and minimum reference prices ($0.28 a pound for refined sugar, $0.23 for other sugar, FOB plant, under the 2020 amendments) and require a Mexican export license for every entry. Sugar under the USDA re-export and polyhydric alcohol programs is outside their scope.

changes.title: 40% IEEPA duty on products of Brazil
changes.detail: +40% on most products of Brazil (9903.01.77) on top of the 10% reciprocal duty. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and higher country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. No Chapter 17 line was on the agricultural exemption list added in November 2025 (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods — most Mexican sugar and candy — were exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 17 goods were **$6.48B in 2025**, 9.7% less than the $7.17B of 2024, the peak year. Half of the total is one product: **sugar confectionery without cocoa (1704.90)**, $3.19B, flat on the year. The drop came from sugar: **raw cane sugar (1701.14)** fell 33% to $1.29B, and imports from **Brazil**, mostly raw sugar, fell 64% to $317M. Raw sugar imports move with the quota and the U.S. crop more than with the tariff: most of it comes in under country allocations at about 1.38¢/kg.

**Mexico** ($1.92B, up 5.6%) and **Canada** ($1.18B, up 7.7%) supplied 48% of 2025 imports — mostly candy, plus Mexican sugar under USMCA and Canadian syrups. The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the Section 301 tariffs from July 24 and the Canada Section 338 duties from August 22, 2026); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on Chapter 17 goods depends as much on **where they come from** as on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico pay no Section 301 duty**, **EU goods pay 10%** in place of a lower base rate, most other large suppliers add 10% or 12.5%, **China adds 20% — 37.5% on refined sugar and most candy** — and **Brazil adds 37.5%**. **In-quota raw and refined sugar is exempt** for every country except Brazil's 25%, and Canadian lactose and syrup blends pay a 50% Section 338 duty. Raw-sugar cells show the polarity rate at 100°, its highest amount; at the usual 96° it is a little lower.

Sugar from Mexico is under antidumping and countervailing duty suspension agreements (export limits, reference prices, export licenses). No antidumping or countervailing duty is collected while they are in force, so the matrix shows none.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 17: Sugars and Sugar Confectionery — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Sugar, Syrups & Candy: Quota Certificates, FDA Rules & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 17) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The USTR, USDA, CBP, Commerce and FDA rules for each HTS Chapter 17 line — sugar quota certificates, re-export licenses, the Mexico suspension agreements, polarity testing, candy safety and labeling — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTA sugar quotas, the WTO quota, re-export programs and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Two sets of rules decide what a Chapter 17 import costs. **Sugar** is managed by the U.S. sugar program: USDA sets the quota quantities, USTR allocates the raw sugar quota among countries and certifies it with certificates of quota eligibility, CBP fills the quotas and tests polarity, and sugar from Mexico must follow the Commerce suspension agreements. **Candy, syrups and other sugars** are food, so **FDA decides whether a shipment can be sold**: the foreign plant must be registered, prior notice filed and a foreign supplier verification program kept — and confectionery has its own hazards, from embedded toys to lead and choking-risk jelly cups.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** or another **FTA** and its sugar quota, enter raw sugar **inside the WTO quota** with a certificate, use the USDA **re-export and polyhydric alcohol programs**, and recover duty through **drawback**. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The Section 301 duty — 10% of value — plus the base rate: Mexican sugar is Free with no quantity limit; Canadian sugar is Free inside Canada's 9,600-tonne quota; USMCA candy, syrups and molasses are Free
levers.appliesTo: All 92 lines, for goods that meet the Chapter 17 rules of origin in General Note 11
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, with the data elements in 19 CFR 182.12; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Sugar, syrups and molasses (1701–1703) qualify only if made from cane or beet grown in the USMCA region (a change from another chapter), so sugar refined from imported raw sugar does not — except Canada's extra refined quota (9823.09.09). Candy (1704) needs only a change from another heading. USMCA does not remove the Section 338 duty on Canadian dairy-list lines, and Mexican sugar must stay within the suspension agreements. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines; on the over-quota sugar lines only Bahrain, Chile, Jordan, Korea, Oman and Singapore are Free without a quota
levers.document: The origin certification or declaration each agreement requires; FTA sugar quotas are filled at CBP, and some need a USTR certificate of eligibility.
levers.caveat: The FTA quotas are small and tied to each partner's sugar trade surplus — for 2026, up to 55,460 t for Guatemala and 40,120 t for El Salvador under CAFTA-DR. An FTA removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty for the 60 economies (U.S. note 52(a)). GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020.

levers.saves: About 32.5¢/kg on raw cane sugar (1.38¢/kg at 96° instead of 33.87¢/kg) and about 32¢/kg on refined sugar (3.66¢/kg instead of 35.74¢/kg) — plus the 10%–12.5% Section 301 duty, because the in-quota lines are exempt from it
levers.appliesTo: Raw cane sugar (1701.13.10, 1701.14.10) from the 39 countries with an FY 2027 allocation; refined and specialty sugar (1701.12.10, 1701.91.10, 1701.99.10, 1702.90.10) under the Canada and Mexico allocations or first-come first-served
levers.document: A certificate of quota eligibility issued by the exporting country's certifying authority, presented at entry for sugar from a country with an allocation; specialty sugar needs a USTR specialty sugar certificate.
levers.caveat: The raw sugar quota is allocated by country — 1,117,195 MTRV for FY 2027 (October 1, 2026 – September 30, 2027), the Dominican Republic, the Philippines, Brazil and Australia holding the largest shares. Brazil's quota sugar still pays the 25% Brazil Section 301 duty. The refined first-come first-served quota (7,090 MTRV) and specialty sugar (1,656 MTRV) fill fast.

levers.title: Use the USDA re-export and polyhydric alcohol programs
levers.saves: The over-quota rate: raw sugar for refining and re-export, for sugar-containing products that are exported, or for making polyhydric alcohols enters under 1701.13.20 / 1701.14.20 at the in-quota polarity rate, outside the quota
levers.appliesTo: 1701.13.20 and 1701.14.20 (raw cane sugar under additional U.S. note 6), and the refined sugar that licensed refiners export
levers.document: A USDA license under 7 CFR part 1530 (the refiner, manufacturer or polyhydric alcohol producer holds it), with the program's records and bond.
levers.caveat: The sugar must be refined and exported, used in exported products, or turned into polyhydric alcohols (not a sugar substitute for food) within the program's time limits; licenses are charged and credited. Sugar under these programs is outside the scope of the Mexico suspension agreements.

levers.title: Use a General Note 15 entry for samples, government or personal-use goods
levers.saves: The over-quota rate: these entries use the "described in general note 15" lines at the in-quota rate and are not counted against the quota
levers.document: Proof of the qualifying purpose: goods for a U.S. government agency; personal-use shipments of 5 kg or less; or samples, trade-fair, research or embassy goods that will not enter U.S. commerce, with written USDA approval presented at entry.
levers.caveat: Commercial goods do not qualify. Ask USDA for approval (identifying the product, quantity and use) before the goods ship.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when the imported goods (or goods made from them, such as candy made with imported sugar) are exported or destroyed
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records.
levers.caveat: Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; check with CBP whether a given Chapter 99 duty is eligible before relying on it. Sugar already under a USDA re-export license cannot also earn drawback on the same use.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification — raw versus refined sugar, a blended syrup versus maple syrup, a sugar-rich article for further processing versus retail candy, white chocolate versus chocolate (1806) — before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the formula, polarity or packaging decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its ingredients, sugar content and packaging.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a reformulated product may need a new one.

groups.note: Raw and refined sugar is the core of the U.S. sugar program: in-quota lines need a certificate of quota eligibility, raw sugar is tested for polarity, sugar from Mexico must follow the suspension agreements, and over-quota sugar can owe a special safeguard duty.

groups.note: Maple syrup, glucose and fructose syrups are ordinary food imports. Blended syrups and sugar-rich articles for further processing have zero quotas (notes 7 and 9) and pay the over-quota rate; in-quota sugar syrups (1702.90.10) share the refined sugar quota.

groups.note: Candy and chewing gum are FDA foods: colors must be listed additives, no embedded toys, no choking-risk jelly cups, and lead is watched closely. Confections for further processing with over 65% or 10% sugar fall on the quota lines.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on sugar imported into the U.S.?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on sugar
what is the tariff on sugar
is there a tariff on cane sugar
faqs.answer: Yes, a two-tier one. Raw cane sugar inside the tariff-rate quota pays 1.4606¢/kg less 0.020668¢/kg for each degree of polarity under 100 — about 1.38¢/kg (0.625¢ a pound) at the usual 96°; above the quota it pays 33.87¢/kg (about 15.36¢ a pound). Refined and beet sugar pay 3.6606¢/kg in quota and 35.74¢/kg above it. On top, the 2026 Section 301 duty (10% or 12.5% for 60 economies) applies to over-quota sugar but not to in-quota sugar, and Brazil pays 25% on both. Mexican sugar is Free under USMCA but limited by the suspension agreements.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for sugar?
faqs.answer: Cane and beet sugar is heading 1701. Raw sugar — a polarimeter reading under 99.5° — is 1701.12 (beet), 1701.13 (non-centrifugal cane sugar of 69° to 93°) or 1701.14 (other raw cane sugar). Sugar with added flavoring or coloring is 1701.91, and refined white sugar and other sugar is 1701.99. The U.S. 8-digit line then depends on quota status: .05 for general note 15 entries, .10 inside the quota and .50 (or .30) above it — for example 1701.99.10 or 1701.99.50 for refined sugar, split into specialty, not-for-further-processing and other sugar at 10 digits.

faqs.question: How does the U.S. sugar tariff-rate quota work?
faqs.answer: USDA sets the quota each fiscal year (October to September) and USTR allocates it. For FY 2027 the raw cane sugar quota is 1,117,195 metric tons raw value, allocated to 39 countries — the Dominican Republic (201,274 t), the Philippines (154,386 t), Brazil (100,000 t) and Australia (94,919 t) have the most. The refined sugar quota is 22,000 t: 10,300 for Canada, 2,954 for Mexico, 7,090 first-come first-served and 1,656 for specialty sugar. Quota sugar needs a certificate of quota eligibility from the exporting country; everything else pays the over-quota rate. FTA partners and Canada have their own sugar quotas, and Mexico has unlimited USMCA access.

faqs.question: What is the U.S.–Mexico sugar suspension agreement, and is there a tariff on Mexican sugar?
faqs.answer: In 2014 Commerce suspended its antidumping and countervailing duty investigations of sugar from Mexico in exchange for two agreements, last amended in 2020: Mexican sugar is sold within yearly export limits, above minimum reference prices ($0.28 a pound for refined sugar and $0.23 for other sugar, FOB plant) and with a Mexican export license for every entry. After the second sunset reviews they were continued in September 2025. As for the tariff: USMCA sugar from Mexico is Free with no quota (9823.09.01) and pays no Section 301 duty; non-USMCA goods pay the base rate plus 10%.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on sugar from Brazil?
faqs.answer: Brazil has a 100,000-tonne raw cane sugar quota for FY 2027. That sugar pays the in-quota polarity rate (about 1.38¢/kg at 96°) plus 25% of value under the Brazil Section 301 action (9903.05.01), which has no sugar exemption; the 12.5% forced-labor duty does not apply to in-quota sugar. Above the quota Brazilian raw sugar pays 33.87¢/kg plus 37.5%. U.S. imports of Chapter 17 goods from Brazil fell 64% in 2025 to $317M (UN Comtrade).

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on sugar from the Philippines?
faqs.answer: The Philippines holds 154,386 metric tons of the FY 2027 raw cane sugar quota. Inside it, the sugar pays only the polarity rate — 20,000 kg at 96° costs $275.59 — because the in-quota lines are exempt from the Philippines' 12.5% Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(b)). Philippine sugar above the quota pays 33.87¢/kg plus 12.5%.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on candy?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on candy
faqs.answer: Yes. Candy without cocoa (hard candy, gummies, lollipops) is 1704.90.35 at 5.6%. On top comes the Section 301 duty by country since July 24, 2026: 10% in total for the EU, 15.6% for the UK and India, 18.1% for Türkiye and Thailand, 43.1% for China (12.5% plus 25% under List 3) and Brazil. USMCA-qualifying candy from Mexico and Canada — more than half of U.S. candy imports — is Free. Chocolate candy is Chapter 18, not Chapter 17.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for candy?
faqs.answer: Sugar confectionery without cocoa is heading 1704. Most candy — hard candy, gummies, jellies, lollipops, marshmallows — is 1704.90.35 (5.6%): .20 for retail candy containing peanuts, .50 for other retail candy, .90 for candy not put up for retail sale. Chewing gum is 1704.10.00, candied nuts 1704.90.10, cough drops 1704.90.25 (Free). Candy that contains cocoa, including chocolate-coated candy, is heading 1806.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for chewing gum?
searchedAs: sugar free chewing gum hs code
faqs.answer: Chewing gum and bubble gum, whether or not sugar-coated, is 1704.10.00 at 4% (1.2% under the U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement, Free under most FTAs and USMCA). Sugar-free gum is a different case: CBP has classified sugar-free chewing gum preparations in 2106.90 (ruling N331050), where the rate is 6.4%.

faqs.question: Is Canadian maple syrup tariffed, and what is its HS code?
faqs.answer: Maple syrup and maple sugar are 1702.20.40 (Free); the 10-digit lines split maple sugar (.10) and syrup by organic status and container size (.40 to .70). Maple syrup is not on the Canada Section 338 lists, so USMCA-qualifying Canadian syrup pays nothing; syrup that does not qualify pays the 10% Section 301 duty for Canada. The 35% IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods ended February 24, 2026. Blended maple syrups for further processing are 1702.20.28 at 16.9¢ per kg of total sugars + 5.1%.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for molasses?
faqs.answer: Molasses from sugar extraction or refining is heading 1703: cane molasses 1703.10 and beet and other molasses 1703.90. Within each, .30 covers molasses imported to extract sugar or for human consumption (0.35¢ a liter) and .50 the rest, mostly feed (0.01¢ per kg of total sugars). Invert molasses is 1702.90.35. Molasses and invert molasses from Canada have been banned since September 29, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for glucose syrup and glucose powder?
faqs.answer: Glucose (dextrose) and glucose syrup with less than 20% fructose in the dry state is 1702.30 — 1702.30.40 at 2.2¢/kg for ordinary glucose syrup and powder. With 20% to 50% fructose it is 1702.40 (5.1%), and over 50% fructose 1702.60 (5.1%). Blended syrups for further processing fall on the zero-quota lines 1702.30.28, 1702.40.28 and 1702.60.28 (16.9¢ or 33.9¢ per kg of total sugars + 5.1%). Glucose meters and test strips are medical products classified elsewhere.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import sugar from?
faqs.answer: In 2025 the largest suppliers of cane and beet sugar (heading 1701) were Mexico ($531M), Brazil ($244M), Guatemala ($172M), the Dominican Republic ($154M), Colombia ($141M), El Salvador ($120M), Australia ($115M) (UN Comtrade, CIF value). Across all of Chapter 17 — $6.48B — candy is the largest product, and Mexico and Canada supplied 48%.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. sugar program?
faqs.answer: A USDA program that supports U.S. sugar prices with loans to processors, marketing allotments that cap domestic sales — 10,574,850 short tons raw value for FY 2027, 85% of forecast consumption — and the import tariff-rate quotas. In July 2026 USDA extended it through crop year 2031 with higher loan rates. Refiners and manufacturers can import sugar outside the quota under the USDA re-export and polyhydric alcohol programs (7 CFR part 1530) if the sugar, or products made with it, are exported.
